txt: Apparently oblivious to his partner's treachery, the uniformed man grabs a ball and takes aim again.
Despite his limp, the man in the uniform moves with efficient grace. His motions are measured and precise.
He catches your glance and nods. "This is the uniform of the Royal Carabineers in service of Frissel the First, Guillaume *Le Lion*, and the valiant King Filippe the Fifth before him."
He gives Gaston a hateful look. "I won her back, but while I was dealing with some... issues..."
He glances at it and frowns. "I prefer the old name -- Insulindian Lily. Girls brought them to young cadets when they entered service. Wearing them on your cap was supposed to bring good luck."
He nods. "I understand. Unfortunately, I don't know what else to tell you. These BM's are an antique. No one uses them anymore. The ammunition is impossible to find."
He nods.
He suddenly remembers *you* are still there, falls silent, and turns away.
His face is motionless like a marble mask. He doesn't comment.
His features stiffen and he gets a cold look. "She... is nobody. This is none of your concern and I refuse to discuss my private affairs with the RCM."
The carabineer crosses his arms and spits in the crater.
The carabineer doesn't reply, but his entire being communicates unbreakable resolve.
The carabineer stares at you with a frown. Doesn't look like he's buying it.
The man in the uniform says nothing. His gaze is fixed on the horizon.
The man shakes his head, mumbling something under his nose, then turns back to you: "Can we get back to our game now?"
The man stares at you, silently frowning.
The old carabineer looks at you with wary expectation.
The old carabineer stands quietly like a statue, his features motionless.
The old carabineer stares at you for a moment, then tension leaves him and he asks: "Was there something else you wanted to take from us?"
The old soldier mumbles something under his breath and turns to face the sea.
The old soldier nods. "Even after the Revolution, after the Beachhead, there was a chance. Had we just stayed true to our *values*..."
The old soldier says nothing, but when his glance quickly runs over Gaston's face, there's an odd look in his eyes.
The old soldier shakes his head in disapproval. "What do you want, officer?"
The old veteran stares at the shot put ball in silence, then speaks in a reserved voice: "What is this? Are you mocking us? This isn't for pétanque."
The veteran extends his right arm with the sun-shaped medal. It glimmers in his wrinkled and scarred palm.
The veteran of numerous armed conflicts extends his right arm with the *Setting Sun* in his clenched fist and an expression of utter disbelief in his eyes.
There's a grimace of pain on the old soldier's face. Looks like he wants to argue, but can't find words. Finally his lips move: "Can we conclude the topic of my guard booth now?"
You catch the old carabineer's gaze slowly leaving his opponent's wrinkled face as his dark eyes meet yours -- whatever turmoil raged in him a moment ago is quelled for now.
"'This time'?!" He's becoming visibly annoyed. "What happened to the first time? Did you make a mistake? Did you *fuck up*? Everyone did!"
"*Bon dieu*," he mumbles, slowly shaking his head. "You and Gaston must be related. His blood runs yellow too."
"*Bon sang*, son. You must have a loose screw up there or something." He taps on his temple. "Sounds like you really mean it."
"*Cop* is a pejorative term. I don't have a problem with policemen. On the contrary, I admire the effort to bring order to our streets."
"*Decisively*. Without fear of offending the sensibilities of the frail and weak-minded among his subjects! This is something the insurgents never understood..."
"*Imbécile, un putain d'imbécile!*..." The old veteran clutches his chest and tries to steady his breathing.
"*Imbécile, un putain d'imbécile*..." The old veteran clutches his chest and tries to steady his breathing.
"*Merde*!" the old soldier yells in outrage. "*Bordel de merde*!!!"
"*Mon dieu*, how much can a man whine, Gaston?"
"*Mon dieu*..." he mumbles, rubbing his temples. "Alright. Alright. Fine. What do you want, officer?"
"*Mon dieu*..." the carabineer closes his eyes, like he's never going to open them again.
"*Now* you are talking sense, son." His eyes light up. "All three of us, working as a group -- we can make a difference."

"*Silence!*" he snaps at Gaston, then turns to you: "Since you put it that way, I *symbolically* accept your cordial gesture." He eats the sandwich-half in two well-measured bites and nods. "For Revachol."
"*Trying* is worth as much as is accomplished. In this case -- almost nothing."
"*You* do not speak his name, craven! Although he was a clown..." he adds. He turns back to you. "But he was *our* clown. Ours to ridicule -- and to mourn."
"...a superpower, feared and respected. A testament to what this country *can* be under the leadership of a True King, someone who knows how to rule."
"A fine example you are setting here today, officer." He says, slowly shaking his head. "I will remember this. And Gaston will too."
"A nation is only as strong *as* its leader. That's why it was such madness to try to..."
"A true King in both blood and mind. Led Revachol before Frissel. He would have been better, but the damn commies drove him into exile."
"AND THEN YOU STOLE HER FROM ME!" He jerks forward, but then grabs his chest and stops.
"Absolutely not." His voice is coarse. "She died of pneumonia in her bed at the age of 79. This is highly... usual."
"Agreed. What about the whole group?" He quickly adds: "I propose *Épées de la Couronne* -- Swords of the Crown, in honour of my old unit."
"Ah, yes, King Filippe III on his steed -- a reminder of what Revachol once was..."

"Alas, the young Drysant was all piss and no vinegar, wearing a tunic of purple velvet and cockatoo feathers to battle." He spits. "Even his rifle was *gold-plated*. Shone from five klicks away. Can you imagine the asininity?"
"All of *this*..." -- he points to you -- "is very unprofessional. Makes me think the Citizens Militia is nothing but a badly organised band of bullies and jesters. Again: I *don't* like this."
"Already got one, smart ass." He utters through his teeth. "Comes with the rank and my service record."
"Alright, I will entertain this... *fantasy*, if you tell me, what interest does an RCM officer have in... 'time travel'?"
"Alright, you got your laugh, ruined my concentration and our game... Anything else you want, or can we start a new one?"
"And I thought getting my knee shattered and surviving on rat carcasses in the trench was bad... here, have one of my medals! You've earned it, *officer*."
"And there are no second chances. We don't deserve them! You can't just go back and restart -- that would make everything *MEANINGLESS*!" A shadow of pain comes over his face.
"Anything else I can assist you with, officer?" he asks impatiently. "We still have a game to finish."
"Anything else you want or can we get back to our game?"
"Are you asking me or telling me?"
"As for the rifle -- I don't know what else to tell you." He shrugs. "These BM446s are an antique. No one uses them anymore. The ammunition is impossible to find."
"Bah!" His gaze wanders over the bay. "There were many such stories in those days. Many such men too. True Revacholians, men with *backbone*."
"Because he was a *god damn* dandy!" he exclaims furiously. "Had no business leading men or even being on the battlefield. All he was, was *related*. That's it."
"Because that's what happens when communards hijack your country, execute your supreme leadership, and turn your capital into a slaughterhouse. You use *heavy ordnance* to clean up your home."
"Because this place is the damn Beachhead," he says, pointing to the bay. "Had to soften the commies up first."
"Build a solid routine and stick to it. That's all there is."
"But as soon as the talk turns real and there's a smallest amount of friction you're suddenly 'not gonna say anything'. Better to be wrong than a goddamn coward!"
"But it's never *only* about love, so what else, officer?"
"But you must agree that Nature, in her infinite wisdom, has made men more fit to perform certain... more *challenging* tasks, don't you, officer?"
"Can you please stop whining for one second and let me take the shot."
"Commies, communists, socialists, anarchists -- call them what you like. They just chose the name to feel special." The carabineer frowns. "Senseless sentimentality."

"Damn Frissel -- he was the king we couldn't protect. The carabineers failed him... and the crown." The old veteran falls silent and massages his chest. "He died in the hands of the *hoi polloi* in a very public execution."
"Damn right, son. They laid the fire of hell on this city before they stormed it. And it worked, too." There is a strange gleam in his eyes.
"Didn't think you had the stomach for it." He nods grimly. "Kids don't these days. I'm used to that."
"Died," he sharply fills the silence and adds: "No use sugar-coating it. Won't bring her back, will it now?"
"Do not *defile* her memory, Gaston." There's an almost imperceptibly small tremble in his voice. "Let her rest in peace."
"Do not speak of what you know nothing about, poltroon!" He slams the heel of his boot in the ground. "*Duty* is something you will never understand."
"Don't get mayonnaise on the measuring tape."
"Enough yacking!" the carabineer cuts Gaston off mid-sentence. "We have a game to finish, so let's get back to it, unless there's something else?"
"Enough," he cuts in sharply. "I can go over these matters *in detail* with you, Gaston, but not while we have company. So officers...?"
"Everyone can see that, yes."
"Everything *you* do reflects on the idea and the people you are representing. When we," he says, pointing to Gaston, "think of the RCM, we think of *you*. Please make it a pleasant thought."
"Exactly what history needs." He spits on the ground between the two of you. "More drifters, confused wanderers, weightless men..."

"Filippe III was even brought into this world with the help of cocaine -- the court medic administered a dose to his mother when she was in labour. And it is well known that with the help of cocaine -- only the purest, of course -- he was able to connect with higher realms..."
"Fine," he snaps at you, obviously annoyed for the interruption. "What is it then?"
"Fine," the carabineer replies sharply. "What do you want now then?"
"Fine. You live, learn, and move on." The former soldier nods in agreement. "The matter is closed. Now what can this old carabineer do for you, officer?"
"Fine." He takes the *boule*. "You tried to right a wrong. It's still a gram better than actual *nothing*."
"For bravery," he interjects.
"For doing my duty in the heat of battle, for looking my mortality in the eye, when men like Gaston here hid in the bushes and shat themselves..."
"Forensic techniques are your forte, not mine, officer." Something stiffens in the man. He shakes his head. "Find another fool, I will not be part of your... joke."
"Forgetting those times means the mistakes were for nothing. That all those people died for nothing."
"From what I've seen of the officers of the RCM..." he begins, looking you over, then stops himself. "But I don't want to get into a debate about drug policies."
"Gender equality is a very noble, very *modern* idea, but in real life, primal roles prevail. But I do not wish to discuss this matter further."
"Goddamn right, son!" The old soldier nods in agreement. "No use complaining about it."
"Goddamn ticker..."
"Goddamnit, son..." He pushes back his cap. "Once you realize Martinaise -- all of Revachol -- is *actually* going to shit, it will be too late."
"Goddamnit, son..." He turns back to you, frowning. "As an officer of the law you should know better than... damn it! Are we done here?"
"Goddamnit..." the old carabineer looks at you, disgusted. "I thought I had you measured, but you can't really measure a slug, can you?"
"Good call." Not a muscle in his face moves as he slowly nods. "Think we can get back to our game now?"
"Good. Gaston finally understands the rules now." An evil smile runs across his lips. "Let's see if it makes him a better *petanquista*."
"Good." He nods. "Mistakes are forgiven, when men at least *try* to right their wrongs. I believe you will try. Now why did you approach us?"
"Have you no shame," the man says to his partner, "whining about your back every time you bring out the measuring tape?"
"He didn't." A shadow of respect crosses his face. "I hoisted the prick on my back and started crawling. Kept going until the 59th Cavalry picked us up."
"He doesn't," the veteran replies sharply. "That was one hundred years ago. Ain't got nothing to do with anything."

"He was the commanding officer and I was on duty. Just doing my job. Shouldn't hand out medals for that..." He shakes his head. "Thirteen months later I received 'The Sun'. For distinguished service. It's not worth mentioning."
"He won't care." The old veteran glances at his partner. "As long as there's food in his fat belly, he'll lick any boot that's kicking it to him..."
"Honour is everything to me," he says with grim finality.
"Hopefully it will finally take your fat ass to the other side of a cardiac arrest, Gaston." His words are slow and deliberate. "This doesn't mean anything. Doesn't *change* anything."
"How about what?!" Judging by his tone the old carabineer really wanted to honour his old unit.
"How are you ever going to get the officer's shit off your nose, Gaston? Or even climb out of his ass?" He shakes his head in extreme disdain.
"How so, then?" He leans in with his hands on his hips.
"I *would* have preferred if the right honourable King Guillaume returned to Revachol or even if that damn clown, Frissel, had risen from the grave and led us. Sadly that was not the case."
"I am merely stating that Nature, in her infinite wisdom, has made men more fit to perform certain... more challenging tasks than women."
"I can't help you officer," he says coldly. "There are no second chances in life. We don't deserve them. This is the world we shaped -- a reflection of what we are. Wasted, ugly, and numb."
"I didn't find it funny."
"I didn't think you had the stomach for it." He nods grimly. "And I can usually tell."
"I do not approve of this *abuse* of power nor your *redistribution* efforts." His features stiffen. "That's not the Revachol *I* fought for. Here..." He hands the sandwich to Gaston.
"I do," he nods, straightening his back. "Fire from heavy artillery."
"I don't care if you are a cop -- you *do not* just ruin someone's game. It's so goddamn disrespectful!"
"I don't mean to keep Gaston's tongue from your rectum, officer, but do you actually have any *police* business with us?"
"I don't want to get into this argument with a police officer," he replies calmly. "Let's just say that in the last eighty-two years I have repeatedly seen my beliefs confirmed in full."
"I doubt it," he remarks dryly. "Anyway, I grabbed the prick and started crawling. Kept going until the 59th Cavalry picked us up."
"I feel 20 years younger every time it rains."
"I got shot in the left shoulder and went down. Just a flesh wound, but just as I turned over, the prince fell into the mud next to me. He was missing his lower jaw."
"I grabbed my sidearm and shot the beast in the head. Then everything went black."
"I hate the socialist rabble," he continues, "but even siding with *them* is better than living your entire life on the fence, never committing to anything. Pick a damn side already!"
"I hope you pass out from it, you goddamn jellyfish. Men like you are the reason this nation is sinking." Standing tall and proud, he looks at his partner with disgust.
"I know the kind," he says with a frown. "Gaston here is the same. A weathervane. Never stood up for anything in his life either."
"I like playing in the dark. Sharpens your nocturnal instincts... Feels like being on recon again."
"I thought you were a busy man, officer. Or at least you should be, so I won't comment on this... eccentricity. Now what?"
"I was 22 when I returned from King Guillaume's Ikeira Operation in the south and found my sweetheart in the arms of this wretch..."
"I'll stop you right there, son." He raises his hand. "I'm old, but I'm not stupid. I *know* a soldier when I see one."
"I'm *not* getting into this with you again." He mumbles through clenched teeth and turns to you. "Officer, was there anything else?"
"I'm an old man, don't sleep more than a few hours every night anyway and... money is tight," he adds with a slight sigh.
"I'm confident they are indispensable in regard to all the paperwork and other administrative duties."
"I'm fine, goddamnit! Mind your own business!" The outburst makes him clutch his chest. "It's nothing, just got to cut back on coffee."
"I'm fine, just a little heart burn..."

"I'm just so damn sorry it had to be the Coalition..." He isn't really paying attention to your words anymore. "After eight years of fighting those hyenas, boiling cats for food and drinking piss in the mountains..."
"I'm listening." He doesn't sound too pleased to have his praises to the miracle of cocaine-fuelled kingship cut short.
"I'm not following you."
"I'm not going to listen to this commie-*connerie*," he utters through clenched teeth and turns his back to you.
"I'm not gonna dignify this with an answer." He frowns. "We're gonna get back to our game now if there isn't anything else, officer?"
"I'm not surprised." He looks at the building. "There are probably lots of forgotten war-time weapons lying around here. Back in the day, everyone had *something* stashed away."
"I'm sorry it had to be them." He looks down at his boots. "After eight years of fighting those hyenas, boiling cats for food and drinking piss in the mountains..."
"I'm sure. But I know this uniform's reputation: You were also wondering if I got these for raping women or killing babies."
"I'm trying to, but you keep breaking my concentration. You're old, I can see that. We're both old. Now stop grabbing your ass like it's a girl."
"I... uh... I..." He looks down at his boots, lips moving, but the words are inaudible.
"If I knew, I would not be *afraid* to tell you. I simply don't. I am an old man, not a coward. The daily business of the riff-raff no longer concerns me."
"If you don't have any more questions we'll return to our game now." By the looks of it he's still trying to wrap his head around what you told him.
"In Martinaise, the Union is the law, so can you really blame them?"

"Instead, all that is just, holy, and beautiful in the world was wiped away and now it's neon signs with toothpaste ads everywhere. Foreign influence peddling garbage and stupid music on the radio." He sighs.
"Is my aim really *that* off?"
"It happened slowly, like a seedling growing into a tree. Tiny incremental steps. Imperceptible till the thicket was so thick you couldn't clear it with a flamethrower..."
"It really does, doesn't it?" The old soldier produces a strange croaking sound -- with laughter-like qualities -- then quickly massages his chest. "But honestly, why?"
"It used to be," he says with a sigh. "But the communards were fond of them, too. Called them *revolutionary* flowers, bells of the Revolution..."
"It was on the first months of the Revolution here in Revachol. Unrest was spreading like wildfire. Marauders had taken most of the Couron and were getting *really* ambitious."
"It's a *Belle-Magrave*," he says, taking the rifle. "4.46 calibre, breech-loading, Revachol-made. Good weapon, accurate and reliable."
"It's a different game in the snow."
"It's a private matter," he says with dignity. "Nothing to do with your investigation."
"It's always about love, isn't it?"
"It's as good a time as any to turn our attention to a different topic, officer," he says, adjusting his cap.
"It's dignified. I like it. We need dignity. And you..." He points to Gaston. "Get excited."
"It's dignified. We need dignity. And you..." He points to Gaston. "Get excited."
"It's no use talking to you. You were still in daddy's balls when it happened. When *we* took our last stand against the filth and rode the cavalry straight into gunfire."
"It's not charity. Not to me..." There's a grimace of pain on the old soldier's face. Looks like he wants to add something, but can't find the words. Finally his eyes light up and he says:
"It's weird. I don't like it. We'll go with mine for now and you..." He points to Gaston. "Get excited."
"King Frissel thought he could end it all in one decisive strike." The old carabineer runs his fingers over the larger medal. "Sent his cousin, Drysant, to put an end to the unrest."
"Look, officer..." He pauses like he doesn't actually know how to reply. "Can we conclude the topic of my guard booth now?"
"Martinaise was used as one of the three footholds in Revachol during Operation Death Blow in '08. The other two are off in Stella Maris and the Delta." He points to the northeast.
"Maybe on some remote parts of the city they do." The old carabineer shrugs. "But I think you have to wait for at least a month."
"Mhmh," he grunts. "Don't get me wrong, officer. I hate those foreign dogs. But the enemy of my enemy and all that. They're the lesser evil."
"Mhmh..." He nods. "We'll get back to our game now if there isn't anything else?"
"NO," the old soldier exclaims sharply. "I don't understand, what you're trying to accomplish with this... sandwich *bonanza*, but I already don't like it." He crosses his arms.

"No -- we were the last ones to keep all the baby killers and rapists in check, and let me tell you, son..." His eyes find yours. "If there hadn't been Royal Carabineers, Revachol might not be standing at all."
"No man can afford to turn his eyes to the horizon if his rear isn't secured. If the womenfolk take care of that, then men can tackle the bigger issues."
"No one. The booth has been unmanned since last Monday." He looks suddenly very old and tired. "There's no other guard. It's just me."
"No point starting this all over again, for the thousandth and the first time. Especially when we have company." He turns to you: "Officer?"
"No reason to even feel bad about that, it's just the way of the animal kingdom."
"No, no you don't! Our pétanque game is ruined!" He's getting angry again. "We want our *boule* back."
"No, they don't. But I'm sorry it had to be the Coalition. After eight years of fighting rabid commies, boiling cats for food and drinking piss in the mountains..." He takes a deep breath.
"No, we are not *good*, goddamnit!" A vein on his forehead is bulging alarmingly. "We want our *boule* back!"
"No," he replies, gaze wondering over the bay. "It was left by heavy artillery fire."
"No," he says without even smiling. "It was left by heavy artillery fire."
"Of course -- don't *sink* into anything. Don't sink into any fight. Only sink into your couch."
"Of course he's holding back." The carabineer crosses his arms. "His mouth is so full of Union prick he can't even speak properly."
"Of course he's not a member! He's not a member of anything. I knew that." He frowns. "He's a weathervane -- turns to where the wind blows and tries to look important."
"Of course there's harm done, you orange slug!" The heel of his cavalry boot slams in the ground. "You owe us a goddamn *boule*!"
"Offic... argh..." He rubs his chest and spits. "Goddamnit... pull yourself together, René." He turns to you. "What do you want?"
"Officer," he says with obvious disdain, "this is unacceptable for anyone bearing an insignia. A man should lead by example, not terror."
"Oh save it." He waves you off. "Men don't have substance anymore, I know that, but seeing such spinelessness in a man bearing an insignia..."
"Our lives are unique, and I have neither the means nor the will to help you change that." A polite nod. "But I will gladly assist you with police matters."
"Please stop."

"Preposterous! Surely you don't mean it." He frowns. "I'm just sorry it had to be them. After eight years of fighting those commie hyenas, boiling cats for food and drinking my piss in the mountains..."
"Probably because those rooster pants are squeezing you senseless. What ever happened to practical? Durable? Revachol-made?" He shakes his head. "Now what can I do for you?"
"Really, officer?" He smirks. "Match an average woman against an average man in a dark alley and see who comes out on top."
"Really?" Suddenly it feels like he's entitled to question you. "What was the unit?"
"Remaining headstrong, making tough decisions on the spot, or even tackling physical obstacles are a few examples of such *challenges*."
"Respects?!" The old carabineer can't believe what he's hearing.
"Revachol Fair of '91 in the Faubourg district." His eyes turn to the sea. "A parade was held to honour Guillaume *Le Lion's* name-day. And the carabineers marched in the place of honour."
"Revachol would be a different place if more people realized that." He gently rubs his chest. "We could still be the..."
"Right, right..." -- he doesn't get sidetracked -- "so I grabbed the prick and started crawling. Kept going until the 59th Cavalry picked us up."
"Right," the old soldier says slowly. "Was the demonstration *it*, or do you still need something from us, officer?"
"Right." The old man stands tall and proud, looking at you inquisitively.

"Royal blood alone doesn't make army commanders. He was a stupid kid, only interested in horses, hair styles, and *manloving*." He spits. "And *seven hundred and eighty two* Royal Carabineers are dead because of his incompetence."
"Sadly, no. It was the foreigners who brought them to their knees. We fought valiantly -- too valiantly. So valiantly we got licked," he adds, squeezing a *boule* in his fist.
"See? Your munching and complaining have ruined my concentration." The man throws a metal ball toward a smaller, wooden ball in the sand, missing it by a metre.

"Should've fought dirty. Like they did with their suicide sex cult propaganda and *mad anarchist women* strapped to shrapnel bombs. We didn't though. And we lacked *calibre*. God bless him, but the suzerain's cannons simply weren't big enough.“
"Six months go by and I realize you must think I've gone blind from all the shrapnel in my head. Because only a blind man wouldn't see through that."
"So I grabbed the *dink*," he says, with a stern look, "and started crawling. Kept going until the 59th Cavalry picked us up."
"So the wind is... yes, perfect."
"Son, we should never forget our past. Lots of mistakes were made back then, but they were also lessons." His voice takes on a tutor-like quality.
"Son..." He's slowly shaking his head. "I don't know why you're feeding me this horse shit, but I'm not biting. Can we get back to our game now?"
"Spring slush on bare feet can make a man feel like a failure." He points at your naked toes. "For a reason. Now, do you need something from us?"
"Stop complaining and hurry up!"
"Strange, I could have sworn..."
"Sure, officer. I am René, René Arnoux, and my *specially abled* partner here is Gaston Martin. How can we help you?" The man in the uniform stands before you tall and proud.
"Sure, officer." Already he looks sceptical. "Let's hear your *take*."
"That's how it is, huh?" The man slowly nods, exhales sharply, and takes the ball. "Fine. I guess you did attempt to right your hooliganism... Consider it forgiven."
"That's just *typical*!" The carabineer looks at you with disgust. "All you young guys these days. You want to be opinionated, controversial, opposition leaders..."
"That's right." The former soldier nods, his fists curling in a ball. "And I'm *sharing* it with you so you can better yourself..."
"That's what I thought." He nods. "We'll get back to our game now if you don't mind, *officer*."
"That's what I thought." He nods. "We'll get back to our game now if you don't mind."
"That's what it was all about?" He takes the sandwich. "Gaston is a snivelling rat -- I've known this my whole life -- but an RCM officer bullying an old man? Robbing him of his meal?!"

"That's why the Filippian kings used cocaine -- for clarity of vision, to aid in their work... Regnum Cocainum -- Revachol's finest years." He seems to grow taller, brimming with pride about the past.
"The 'right track'? This *is* the right track! The only track." He gets visibly annoyed. "This is the world we shaped, a reflection of what we are: cowardly, ugly, and numb."
"The *possibility* of someone being in there is enough to discourage any ill-minded individuals..." he tries to argue.
"The Suzerain is the King. Has everyone forgotten already?" He then slowly nods and says to himself: "They've forgotten already."
"The best, huh?" he says inspecting the ball. "This isn't even a *boule*, but... Fine. I guess you did attempt to right your hooliganism... Consider it forgiven."
"The dink had taken numerous flesh wounds and lost a lot of blood, but despite missing his jaw he seemed hesitant to die. Tougher than he looked, that one."
"The only one you have."
"The purity of snow always reminds me of the purity of a man's soul...." He looks at the falling snow. "If he's got principles."
"The rebels were smart. They let us come real close before opening fire. Suffice to say, it was carnage."
"The rest of the city got cleaned up, but Martinaise they keep as a *monument*." A dark shadow runs across his face. "And now the Union socialists are practically running the place."
"The twelve-year-old junkie, whose alcoholic father beats him?" His eyes light up. "Why did you do that?"
"Then help him, you wimp." Reproach fills his eyes. "You rub plenty of shoulder with the *gauche caviar* in the Union. Someone *must* know something."
"Then his horse, driven mad by the noise and smell of gunpowder, stepped on my leg and shattered my knee." He pats his right thigh.
"There's no point in getting angry at nature, officer. This is just the way we are *made*."
"There's nothing for you to *understand* here," he snaps. "It is not *her* death you are investigating."
"They're *not*. And I'm sorry it had to be them. After eight years of fighting those hyenas, boiling cats for food and drinking piss in the mountains..." He takes a deep breath.
"This deity of yours has quite the following in Martinaise..." He straightens his back. "None as zealous as you it seems, though."

"This here is blood ground, where Coalition boots first made landfall and cleaned those rabid dogs out. Most likely," he says, looking down at the soil, "we're playing pétanque on their mangled corpses."

"This place is the damn Beachhead, son," he says, pointing to the bay. "They had to soften the commies up first."
"This was the happiest day of my life." This is said in such a matter-of-fact tone, it leaves no room for doubt.
"Through some miracle we both survived. And the jawless freak convinced Frissel to give me a medal for not leaving him to die in his own blood, piss, and shit."

"To keep the long and bloody story short, Drysant marched us against the partisans in Couron. And when I say 'marched', I mean made us walk into captured enemy territory single-file, like toy soldiers, while he rode in front on his giant red stallion."
"Ugh..." The old man looks at you, obviously annoyed by the interruption. "Sure. Yes. Yes, you can ask your questions."
"Unbelievable... How can you even walk up straight with that liquid backbone of yours, Gaston?" He shakes his head. "Officer, what do you want?"
"Unfortunately, I don't." He shrugs. "Unlike most of the locals, I have no qualms about assisting law enforcement, but this affair has passed me by completely."
"Up there I give it all I got. I *earn* my keep." He looks towards the guard booth and sighs. "But you're right officer, there is no middle ground. It's do or die."
"Vigilance, officer!" He salutes you. "What can this old carabineer do for you?"
"W-war?" The word seems to derail his train of thought. "I mean yes. Yes... It changes men, changes lives and uh..."
"Was the vessel you boarded the 'HMS Commodore Red'?"
"Was there anything else, officer?" he asks impatiently. Looks like they both want to continue the game.
"Watch out, Gaston..." He points at you. "It's Inspector Oaf. Come to throw more of our stuff into the sea, officer?"
"We were just boys, then. This was different. *You*..." The tall veteran looks at you and nods.
"We'll get back to our game now if you don't mind."
"We're still waiting for a replacement for the *boule* you sent sinking."
"Well, I'm glad at least some people bearing your insignia have kept a level head in these turbulent times."
"Well, it damn well isn't, it's pétanque," the man snaps, raising his voice again. "You ruined a pétanque game. We want our *boule* back!"
"Wh...? Oh, I see." He takes a step back and nods, jaw clenched tight. "You're a comedian after all. Funny guy. *Unpredictable*."
"What do *you* know about history?" The carabineer snaps at Gaston. "You never witnessed history. Only heard about it -- years later -- when it had already moved on. You don't know history."
"What else?"
"What the HELL is your problem?"
"What the hell are we talking about here, officer?" He rubs the back of his head. "Look, we just want to play our game, so unless there's something else..."
"What?!" The old soldier scowls at you, unamused.
"When I came to, it was all over," he continues, ignoring his companion. "It was just me and jawless Drysant, gurgling in the blood-soaked mud right next to me."
"When the dissidents come to *rape* our country, he hides, but try to get a bite of his dear sandwich and he gets claws? You're a special kind of a vermin, Gaston."
"Where he tells his little *penman* exactly what to say! It's commie propaganda, plain and simple. You should be ashamed of yourself."
"Where?!" His head drops between his shoulders he snaps around with surprising speed.
"Who did you think you were fooling with your moaning, Gaston?" He doesn't even glance at his partner.
"Why don't the two of you get a tomb and take your whining there." He looks at you, disgusted. "I am ashamed to even stand in the same crater with you."
"Why what?"
"Will this...." He falls silent and stares at the ball. "No, it will *goddamn* not..."
"Wouldn't even pick it up, if my heart wasn't in it."
"Yes, dammit -- I know! They laid the fire of hell on this city before they stormed it. And it worked, too." There is a strange gleam in his eyes.
"Yes, from the looks of it you deserve a medal for the *excellent* handle you have on things." He snorts. "Here, have one of mine!"
"Yes, pétanque," the man says, raising his voice again. "You ruined our pétanque game. We want our *boule* back."
"Yes, that's what you need, Gaston. More padding on that fat ass of yours. I hope your heart gives out."
"Yes, the Débardeurs' Union pays me to stand vigil during the nights." He looks down. "Not out of any *political* allegiance, mind you."
"Yes, yes, yes," the carabineer utters angrily. "Can we conclude the topic of my guard booth now?"
"Yes, yes. Like I said," he brings it up again, "I would be up *anyway*, so might as well keep an eye out. It keeps my senses sharp."
"Yes," he nods, inspecting you with some disdain. "The military-coordinated amphibious landing to take back Revachol."
"Yes," he replies with a reluctant nod. "It was left by heavy artillery fire."
"Yes," he says impatiently. "I was standing right here. I saw it. Why are you telling me this?"
"Yes. It does." He nods. "Unfortunately I wasn't working that night. Been on a two-week leave since last Monday."
"Yes..." The man nods. "The terrain here provides an interesting variety to a familiar game."
"Yes." He nods, before hesitantly continuing. "It's... it's not actually an issue. I mean..."
"You always confused her, couldn't let us be happy..." He says with heavy resentment. "Seduced her with your fancy words and *pastries*."
"You are representing an organisation, an insignia, an idea." The old man continues in a softer tone. "You need to understand that."
"You can't even take responsibility for yourself -- how could you fathom the responsibility weighing on the shoulders of a ruler?" he asks, obviously annoyed.
"You don't even *begin* to truly understand the players on the table, let alone the specific circumstances surrounding the..." He stops mid-sentence and turns to you. "What do you think?"
"You haven't lived as long as I have, son. With age, a man learns certain things about real power -- or else ends up a spineless socialist rat, like Gaston here."
"You know what..." He falls silent and the emerging smile withdraws. "No. They brought me misery, false hope, and disappointment. The *revolutionaries* sullied them."
"You mean alcohol?"
"You stole her from me," René repeats, trying to steady his breathing and still clutching his chest.
"You vandalized our game, son." He tries to calm himself. "We can't play pétanque with five *boules*."
"You were a rat when we were boys and you are a rat now. Of course I knew!" He spits. "Your deception was so bad at first I thought you were play-acting for my amusement."
"You're talking about getting black-out shitfaced drunk and going into delirium, right?" he asks impatiently.
